title: AFTER DELETE Triggers and Audit Records
learningObjectives: Explain when an AFTER DELETE trigger runs.
Use OLD values to capture a deleted row's information.
Create an audit table and populate it from a DELETE trigger.
Describe why delete audits need retention and access controls.
Recognize that cascade-trigger behaviour must be checked for the target DBMS.

understand.concept: A DELETE trigger can record information about a row that is being removed. In an AFTER DELETE trigger, OLD contains the deleted row's values and can be copied to an audit table.
understand.whyItMatters: Deletion audits help trace data removal, support compliance and explain why records are no longer present in an operational table.
understand.analogy: A trigger is like an automatic rule attached to a data event: it runs when the specified change occurs, even if the application did not call it directly.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model OLD/NEW row values, transaction timing, recursive execution or DBMS-specific trigger semantics.

explain.narrative:
## AFTER DELETE
An AFTER DELETE trigger runs after a row has been deleted. OLD exposes the deleted row's values; there is no NEW row for a DELETE event.

## Audit design
A delete audit can preserve the deleted key, a few relevant fields and an action label. Avoid copying sensitive fields unless the retention and access policy explicitly requires them.

## Cascades and triggers
Foreign-key cascades can cause additional row changes. Understand whether the target DBMS fires triggers for cascaded actions and test the exact engine/version. Do not assume identical behaviour across products.

### Deleted-row values
For DELETE triggers, OLD contains the row being removed and NEW is not available. An AFTER DELETE trigger can copy OLD values into an audit table after the delete operation has taken place. Because the audit row is written in the same transaction, rolling back the transaction also rolls back the audit insert.

### Privacy and retention
Audit tables can preserve personal or commercially sensitive data beyond the lifetime of the live row. Define access controls, retention periods and lawful deletion procedures before using this pattern in production.

examples.title: Create a member table
examples.code: CREATE TABLE trg17_members (member_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, member_name TEXT NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL);
examples.explanation: Creates the live member table. Its status is required, and member_id identifies each member.

examples.title: Create a deletion audit table
examples.code: CREATE TABLE trg17_member_deletes (audit_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, member_id INTEGER NOT NULL, member_name TEXT NOT NULL, old_status TEXT NOT NULL);
examples.explanation: Creates an audit table that copies the deleted member's identifier, name and former status. It has no foreign key to trg17_members because the referenced live row is expected to be deleted.

examples.title: Insert a member
examples.explanation: Seeds a member row so the DELETE trigger has a concrete OLD row to inspect.

examples.title: Create an AFTER DELETE trigger
examples.code: CREATE TRIGGER trg17_member_delete AFTER DELETE ON trg17_members BEGIN INSERT INTO trg17_member_deletes(member_id, member_name, old_status) VALUES (OLD.member_id, OLD.member_name, OLD.status); END;
examples.explanation: Creates an AFTER DELETE trigger. Once a member is deleted, OLD.member_id, OLD.member_name and OLD.status still expose the values from the deleted row, allowing the trigger to preserve an audit snapshot.

examples.title: Delete the member and inspect the audit
examples.code: DELETE FROM trg17_members WHERE member_id = 1; SELECT member_id, member_name, old_status FROM trg17_member_deletes;
examples.explanation: Deletes only member_id 1 and then reads the audit table. The output verifies both effects: the live row is removed and its former values are retained in the audit table. In production, restrict audit access because copied personal data may be sensitive.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples and verify that the operational member row is removed while the minimal audit record remains.
practise.independentTask: Create an inventory table and a delete-audit table. Add an AFTER DELETE trigger that records the item ID and a non-sensitive description.
hints: A DELETE trigger has OLD values but no NEW row.
AFTER DELETE runs after the row is removed.
Copy only the fields needed for traceability.
Consider audit retention, privacy and access controls.
Test foreign-key cascade behaviour on the target database engine.

questions.prompt: What does OLD represent in a DELETE trigger?
options: The next row in sort order
questions.explanation: OLD exposes the values of the deleted row.

questions.prompt: Is there a NEW row in a DELETE trigger?
options: Only when a primary key exists
Only when the table has an index
questions.explanation: DELETE removes a row, so it has OLD values but no NEW row.

questions.prompt: What is a common purpose of an AFTER DELETE trigger?
options: Record a minimal audit entry for the deleted row
Run a SELECT on every table
questions.answer: Record a minimal audit entry for the deleted row
questions.explanation: An AFTER DELETE trigger can preserve an audit record.

questions.prompt: Why should audit data be minimized?
options: To make triggers run before insert
questions.explanation: Audit records should contain only the information required by policy.

questions.prompt: What should be verified for cascaded deletes?
options: The target DBMS's trigger behaviour for foreign-key cascades
questions.answer: The target DBMS's trigger behaviour for foreign-key cascades
questions.explanation: Cascade and trigger interaction can vary across products and must be tested.
